title: How Do I Hold My People Accountable?
author: Joel
source: Managing the Future on Substack, December 18, 2025
summary: The author opens on a paradox every leader faces: the more you believe in a person, the more they let you down, because belief without accountability becomes license. The move is to hold people accountable not from suspicion but from care. The piece reframes accountability as clarity about what is expected, what success looks like, what the consequences are for falling short, and what support is available. When a leader dodges these conversations because they like the person or fear the person will be hurt, they are not being kind; they are withholding the information that person needs to succeed. The practical frame is that accountability conversations are not punishment conversations; they are clarity conversations. The leader names what is expected, asks what obstacles the person is hitting, and offers the support they need to meet the standard. If they still cannot meet it after support, the conversation shifts. But the first conversation, the one most leaders avoid, is the one where you name clearly what the standard is and ask what the person needs to hit it.
points: Belief without accountability becomes license; the more you believe in a person, the more you have to hold them accountable, from care not from suspicion.
Accountability is clarity: what is expected, what success looks like, what consequences are for falling short, what support is available; it is not punishment.
Leaders who dodge accountability conversations because they like someone are not being kind; they are withholding the information that person needs to succeed.
quotes: How do I hold my people accountable?” is the #1 question I get from the CEOs I teach. The answer is relatively simple, but it's not easy and it requires a pretty involved process.

The accountability process begins before you ever hire someone. It starts with you answering two questions: What job needs to be done? Who fits that role best? Making sure your hire has the right aptitude and motivation is critical. You can't hold someone accountable for work they don't have the skills to perform or the motivation to engage in.” “Once you've hired the right person, the next step in the accountability process is micro-training. Too many businesses skip this entirely, then act surprised when the new hire doesn't do things the way they want.
Now, you need to document their responsibilities and key metrics in what I call an Executive Performance Profile. This step, too, gets skipped or glossed over all the time, but it's essential.
At these meetings, ask each employee: “How likely are you to achieve these goals on time?” Notice we're asking for a prediction, not a progress report. This may seem subtle, but it's crucial.

If you let employees just feed you data, “Hey boss, I'm 10% done… 20% done… 50% done”, they're not taking accountability for delivering the result. They're just reporting progress, which means you're the one ultimately accountable.
There are good reasons a goal might not be achieved. But there are very few good reasons someone didn't know they weren't going to achieve it.

The main thing I want to communicate here is that so many managers (CEOs included) jump straight to the accountability conversation without laying this foundation. That's unfair to the employee and to the organization. … That works a hell of a lot better than hire → hope → retaliate.” Archived from Managing the Future on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
